title: The Hajj of the heart
hook: those who can't go share in it by fasting Arafah and by longing

segments.voice: Yesterday: visiting Medina, and peace sent on the Prophet from near or far. Your line: peace on you, messenger.

They came asking for something to ride. An expedition was setting out, and these men wanted to go, but they had no mount and no money for one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them he had nothing to carry them on. Surah At-Tawbah keeps what happened next. They turned away, their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they couldn't find the means. The Qur'an says there is no blame on them. They stayed home. Their tears went on the record anyway. Today, the Hajj of the heart.
screen: `NOTHING TO RIDE.` → `EYES OVERFLOWING.` → `NO BLAME ON THEM.`

segments.voice: This path began the pilgrimage with a condition: the Hajj is due on those who can find a way. Today is for everyone else. First, the men in tears. The verse doesn't scold them for staying home. It names their grief and lifts the blame. Wanting to go and being unable is different from not wanting to go. Second, the people left behind. Anas reports, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that on the way home from that expedition the Prophet told his companions: there are people in Medina who were with you on every road you traveled and every valley you crossed. They were held back by an excuse. Held back, and still with you. Third, a rule of thumb from the same collection. When a servant of God falls ill or travels, the Prophet said, the good he used to do while healthy and at home is still written for him. The record follows habit and intention, not just location. Fourth, what people at home actually do. On the day of Arafah, while the pilgrims stand on the plain, Muslims who aren't there are encouraged to fast, and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet's praise for that fast. And in the first days of Dhul Hijjah, a person who plans to offer a sacrifice is told, in another report in Muslim, to leave their hair and nails uncut until it's done, a small echo of the pilgrim's restraint, kept at home, far from Mecca. So while the plain fills, someone in an ordinary kitchen keeps the fast: their share of the day.
screen: `IF THEY CAN FIND A WAY.` · `TEARS, AND NO BLAME.` · `HELD BACK, AND STILL WITH YOU.` · `FASTING ARAFAH FROM HOME.` · then, large: `THEY WERE HELD BACK BY AN EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, ask God in your own words for the chance to go one day, or for someone you love to go, plainly, the way the men who came asking for a mount asked. If you don't, think of a place you've always wanted to stand in and couldn't yet, and let yourself want it, unhurried.
The Hajj of the heart. Taking part from home, by longing, by fasting on the day of Arafah, and by the intention of those who are held back by an excuse. Today's word.
screen: `THE HAJJ OF THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: longing counts. Being held back is not the same as staying away. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Muslims who cannot make the pilgrimage may fast on the day of Arafah, say the takbir through the first days of Dhul Hijjah, offer a sacrifice at Eid al-Adha if able, and ask God for the chance to go.

chat.says: I can't afford to go on Hajj. Does my wanting to go count for anything?
options: Yes. The Qur'an lifts blame from those who long to go but lack the means.
Not really. Only the pilgrims who actually stand at Arafah get any reward.
Only once you've saved enough; until then the wish means nothing.
chat.meaning: Surah At-Tawbah lifts the blame from men who wept because they couldn't go, and the Prophet said those held back by an excuse were still with them.

Arafah.meaning: the plain outside Mecca where pilgrims stand on the ninth

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of the Prophet's sayings and deeds

notes: 9:92 is paraphrased (the men who came asking for mounts and turned away weeping). Commentators connect it to the Tabuk expedition; the script says only 'an expedition'.
Bukhari 2839 (also 4423, Anas, returning from Tabuk): 'people in Medina... held back by an excuse'. Confirm number.
Bukhari 2996 (Abu Musa): the ill and the traveler credited with what they used to do. Confirm.
Muslim 1162: the fast of Arafah; the expiation of two years is deliberately not stated here (taught on day 1114).
Muslim 1977: one intending to sacrifice leaves hair and nails from the start of Dhul Hijjah. Schools differ on whether this is obligatory or recommended; confirm phrasing 'is told'.
Practice invites asking 'in your own words' if you pray; no new prayer written.
